record.passage: For two days Marek and Santiago had been trading short, cold messages about a missed football practice. At 9 p.m., sitting on his bed in Warsaw with the heater ticking, Marek typed and deleted three angry replies. Then he wrote: 'Can I call you? I think we misunderstood each other.' The reply came fast: 'ok.' The phone rang. For a second neither spoke. Then Santiago said, 'So when you wrote "fine, whatever"...' and Marek groaned. 'I meant, like, oh well! Not I hate you!' 'It read like you hated me!' 'And you wrote "I have a life too"!' 'Because I thought you hated me!' There was a pause, then both burst out laughing. Five minutes in, two days of hurt felt ridiculous.

qa.a: He typed and deleted three angry replies.

qa.q: What does the burst of laughter show about how both felt once they heard each other?
qa.a: It shows relief; hearing each other's voices made the hurt feel silly, as each realised the other had never meant to attack.

qa.a: Instead of another cold text, he suggested a call and named the likely misunderstanding, which invited Santiago in without blame.

qa.a: Probably nervous and a bit defensive at first, then relieved once he could hear Marek's real tone 😊.

I'm Neelam, Gargi's roommate, and for five weeks I've watched her "almost start" her internship application essay.
First she read every past winner's essay she could find. Then she made a colour-coded spreadsheet of their structures. Then she bought a book on persuasive writing and underlined half of it. Her outline is taped to our wall, and every night she moves the sticky notes around.
Yesterday I asked, "How much have you written?"
"Nothing yet, but the structure's nearly perfect." She sounded proud, even cheerful.
But when I offered to read a rough paragraph, she went very still. "Not until it's ready. I don't want anyone seeing a bad version."
I can't know what's going on in her head. From outside, it looks as if she's working all the time.
The deadline is Sunday.

By the third month, the small bets on the phone game did nothing for Nitin anymore. Only bigger ones made his chest go loose the way the first ones had.

I'm Divyansh, and last year I thought "lazy" was just my name. Every evening I sat with my maths book and looked out of the window, and Mummy said, "Lazy boy, again?" Papa said it too. After a while I said it myself: "I can't, I'm lazy." It felt true, like being short.

Subject: You were right about 'safe accounts'

Hi Thomas,
Weird week. On Tuesday someone rang saying they were from my bank's fraud team. They knew my name and the last four digits of my card. They said my account was compromised, that I had to move my savings to a 'safe account' before midnight, and not to tell anyone because 'the fraudster might be close to you'.

So I hung up mid-sentence, opened the bank's own app and called from there. They froze the transfer and said calling within the hour really helped. Then I rang the fraud reporting line and told my flatmate, who made me toast and sat with me.
Still shaky, but mostly okay. Thank you for that random lecture last year.
Noor

record.passage:
I'm Ritu. I've been staying with my sister Nikita and Gautam for my internship, sleeping on their sofa-bed, so I hear more than I should.
For weeks they'd been polite. "Dinner?" "Ate at work." "Okay." Then on Thursday night, while I pretended to sleep, Nikita switched off the TV.
"Gautam," she said, very gently, "I feel like we're drifting apart, and I don't know how to find our way back. I'm not angry. I just miss us."
There was a long silence. I held my breath.
Then Gautam said, "I've felt it too. I didn't know how to say it." His voice cracked a little.
They talked till past one. I heard words like "counselling" and "maybe" and "what do you want". I don't know what they decided. But the next morning they made tea together, for the first time since I arrived.

qa.q: Why is Ritu staying with Nikita and Gautam?
qa.a: Ritu is staying with them for an internship, sleeping on their sofa-bed.

qa.q: What did Gautam's cracking voice suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Gautam was relieved and emotional that Nikita had named the drift he had felt but couldn't say.

qa.q: What made Nikita's way of naming the drift helpful?
qa.a: Nikita said it gently, without blame, and said she missed them, which opened a real talk about counselling and what each of them wants.

qa.q: How does Ritu see the change the next morning?
qa.a: Ritu notices them making tea together for the first time, a small sign that the honest talk shifted something, even without knowing their decision.

record.grounding: Shows one partner kindly saying aloud that they are drifting, opening a talk about counselling, repair or an honest parting.

row_description: On returning, each restates the other's point before their own and owns their harshest words. They leave with one small practical agreement, like a rota, because a shared plan holds better than a shared feeling.
recipe_text: A chat or text-message exchange (short lines), with a few narrator words only if needed; emojis may appear as real people use them.

row_description: A parent notices a teen's changed friends, moods and secrecy and reacts with alarm or punishment. Calm curiosity about what the substance or habit does for them opens honest talk, which lasts longer than fear.
recipe_text: A diary or journal entry by the protagonist, written the same day, informal.

record.passage:
Wednesday night
Found Tanvir gaming at 2:40 am again, headphones on, lit blue by the screen. My first thought was to yank the charger out of the wall. I actually had my hand on it.
Then I remembered how that went in January: he screamed, I screamed, and he just played at his friend Neil's house instead.
So tonight I sat on the edge of his bed and waited for the round to end. Then I asked, "What does it give you, beta? Honestly."
He looked at me as if I'd grown two heads. Then he said, "When I'm playing, nobody at school is laughing at me."
I didn't know anyone was laughing at him. I didn't know any of it.
I said, "Thank you for telling me. Let's talk more tomorrow after school. Sleep now?" He actually nodded.
Tomorrow: call his class teacher about the teasing. Keep my voice calm.
Damini

qa.q: What time did Damini find Tanvir gaming?
qa.a: At 2:40 am.

qa.q: Why did Damini stop with a hand on the charger?
qa.a: Damini remembered that yanking it in January led to screaming and Tanvir playing at Neil's house instead, so punishment hadn't worked.

qa.q: What does Damini plan for tomorrow, and why is it a good next step?
qa.a: To call the class teacher about the teasing and keep a calm voice, which deals with the reason Tanvir escapes into games, not just the gaming.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Tanvir to be asked 'What does it give you?'
qa.a: He may have been surprised to be asked instead of scolded, and it gave him a chance to admit that classmates were laughing at him.

record.grounding: Illustrates a parent resisting a punishing reaction to late-night gaming and asking calmly what it gives the teen, which reveals the teasing behind it.

row_description: She vents to her sister, who says "he always does this", strengthening her anger. A well-meaning listener can turn a passing quarrel into a settled verdict without hearing the other side.
recipe_text: An elder (grandparent, uncle, senior colleague) tells the story to a younger person as a memory or example, in their voice.

record.subtype: Stage 4: Family or friends pulled in [Observer]
record.passage: Darshan, you're newly married, so let your Urmila Nani tell you something I watched with my own eyes. When your mother was twenty-five, she had a silly text fight with your father, something about who forgot the gas bill. She phoned her sister, your Meenu Masi, from my verandah. I was shelling peas nearby. Meenu listened for two minutes and said, 'He always does this. Always. Don't let him treat you like that.' I watched your mother's face change. Before the call she was annoyed. After it, she was certain. It wasn't about a gas bill any more; it was about what kind of man he was. Meenu meant well; she loved her sister. But she'd heard only one side.

qa.q: What was Urmila doing while her daughter was on the phone?
qa.a: She was shelling peas nearby.

qa.q: How did the mother's feelings change during the call with Meenu?
qa.a: She went from mildly annoyed to angrily certain, as Meenu's 'he always does this' turned a small quarrel into a judgement of her husband.

qa.q: What could Meenu have said instead that would have helped?
qa.a: She could have listened, asked what he said about it, and suggested talking to him directly, rather than giving a verdict on hearing one side.

qa.q: How might Darshan's father have experienced that evening?
qa.a: He probably came home to a wife far angrier than a gas bill deserved, without knowing a verdict about him had been reached in his absence.

record.grounding: A grandmother recalls watching her daughter vent to her sister, whose 'he always does this' turned a small text quarrel into a settled verdict.

row_description: She wants to expose a secret of her own or cut the friend off entirely. The wise move is to wait a day, since revenge will make her the one on the wrong side of the story.
recipe_text: An observer's account: a neighbour, sibling, classmate or colleague describes what they saw, without knowing the protagonist's inner state for sure.

record.subtopic: Friendship betrayal to reconciliation or ending
record.subtype: Stage 4: Anger, retaliation urge and withdrawal [Receiver]
record.passage:
I'm Nathan, Elizabeth's older brother, and I've never seen her the way she was on Tuesday. She came home, dropped her bag in the hallway and went straight to her laptop. When I looked over her shoulder, she was typing a post about Anjali, something about Anjali's mum and the shop. Her jaw was tight and her hands were quick.
"She told everyone about me," she said without looking up. "So now everyone gets to know about her."
I don't know everything that happened between them. I just said, "Lizzie, can you wait till tomorrow? Right now you're the one who got hurt. Post that and you're the one who did the hurting."
She glared at me. Then she deleted the draft, blocked Anjali's number instead, and lay face-down on the sofa for an hour. I made her toast. I can't tell if she's angry or just really sad.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth do instead of posting?
qa.a: Elizabeth deleted the draft and blocked Anjali's number instead.

qa.q: Why did Elizabeth want to post about Anjali?
qa.a: Elizabeth was furious that Anjali told everyone about her and wanted Anjali to feel the same exposure.

qa.q: Why was waiting a day a wise suggestion?
qa.a: Anger that strong usually cools a little overnight; posting Anjali's secret would have made Elizabeth the one who did harm, while waiting keeps her choices open.

qa.q: How does Nathan see Elizabeth's evening?
qa.a: Nathan sees how upset his sister is but can't tell whether she is angry or deeply sad, so he stays near and makes her toast.

record.grounding: Shows a hurt teenage girl wanting to expose her friend's secret or cut her off, and a brother urging her to wait a day so she does not become the wrongdoer.

row_description: One friend gets a placement in another city, another falls into a relationship, a third struggles with money. Calls turn into likes on posts, and both feel guilty for being the one who did not call.
recipe_text: First-person reflective account by the protagonist, looking back a little (for 7-12 keep it simple and short).

record.passage:
I'm Jasleen. After final year, our trio split three ways. I got a placement in Bengaluru. Rajni met a guy from her office in Delhi and suddenly had plans every weekend. Noor stayed back home and took tuition batches to help pay her brother's fees, so she was always tired.
At first we did Sunday video calls. Then every other Sunday. Then someone would cancel, usually me, because of a deadline. Now I mostly know Rajni's life through her posts. I like them. She likes mine.
Last month I saw her birthday photos and realised I hadn't called. I felt sick with guilt.
Then Rajni messaged: "Sorry I've gone missing, I keep meaning to call you." She felt it too. Neither of us had stopped caring. We just both kept waiting to be the one with free time.

qa.q: Where did Jasleen get a placement?
qa.a: Jasleen got a placement in Bengaluru.

qa.q: What did Jasleen feel on seeing Rajni's birthday photos, and why?
qa.a: Jasleen felt sick with guilt on realising there had been no call on Rajni's birthday.

qa.q: What could Jasleen and Rajni try so the friendship doesn't live only in likes?
qa.a: They could set a short, fixed call time that suits both schedules, or send voice notes, instead of waiting for free time that never comes.

qa.q: How is Rajni experiencing the same drift?
qa.a: Rajni feels guilty too: her message 'I keep meaning to call you' shows she still cares but is caught up in her new life.

record.grounding: Shows college friends scattering to a new city, a relationship and money struggles, with calls turning into likes and guilt on both sides.

row_description: After a harsh argument over his course, he moves out and says he does not wish to be contacted. Part of him is relieved and part is terrified, and pride makes the decision feel final.
recipe_text: Dialogue-heavy scene (mostly spoken lines, little narration): a family or home scene when the counterpart is family; otherwise set where that relationship naturally happens (class, office, team, street), still mostly dialogue.

record.passage:
"Mohit, put the bag down. Please."
"I'm done, Ma. You heard what he said about my course."
"He was angry. He says things when he's angry."
"He said I'm throwing his money down the drain. In front of everyone."
"So you'll just leave? Where will you even stay?"
"At the hostel. I've paid the first month myself."
Sudha held the door frame. "At least call me."
Mohit's zip jammed; he yanked it hard. "Tell him not to contact me. I mean it."
"And me?"
He stopped. His voice went small. "I don't know, Ma."
Outside, the auto honked. He picked up the bag, looking almost relieved and almost scared.
"I'm not coming back to beg," he said, and went down the stairs.

qa.q: Where does Mohit say he will stay?
qa.a: At the hostel; he has paid the first month himself.

qa.q: What does Mohit's voice going small at "And me?" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests that under his anger he is scared of losing his mother too, even as pride pushes him out the door.

qa.q: What turning point could Sudha offer in this moment?
qa.a: She could tell him calmly that her door stays open and ask only that he let her know he's safe, keeping one thread alive without forcing him to stay.

qa.q: What is Sudha experiencing as Mohit goes down the stairs?
qa.a: She is likely frightened and heartbroken, caught between her son and the harsh words at home, and unsure whether Mohit will ever call.

record.grounding: After a harsh argument about his course, a young man leaves and asks not to be contacted, relieved and scared at once, with pride sealing the choice.

row_description: Each child recounts the story so that only the other is at fault. Voices rise, "you always" and "you never" appear, and neither is listening because both are busy preparing the next defence.
recipe_text: Scene set inside an institution: school, hostel, clinic waiting room, workplace, sports club, community centre.

record.passage: In the corridor outside the Class 5 staff room, Wasim and Devika stood by the water cooler, both red in the face. The cricket bat between them had a crack along the handle. "Devika threw it on the ground after her turn, Ma'am, I saw!" "No, Wasim hit the wall with it! You always blame me for everything." "And you never admit anything!" Mrs Kulkarni, the games teacher, opened her mouth, but Wasim was already talking again, listing every broken thing from last term. Devika wasn't listening; her lips were moving as she got her next answer ready. Neither of them looked at the bat anymore. It had become a contest over who would get the last word.

qa.q: What was wrong with the cricket bat?
qa.a: The cricket bat had a crack along the handle.

qa.q: What do Devika's moving lips suggest about what was in her mind?
qa.a: She was getting her next answer ready instead of listening, so her mind was on defending herself, not on understanding Wasim.

qa.q: How could Mrs Kulkarni turn this moment around?
qa.a: She could set the bat aside, ask both children to drink some water, and give each a turn to speak without interruption before deciding anything.

qa.q: If you were Mrs Kulkarni, what would you notice about the argument?
qa.a: The teacher would notice that neither child looks at the bat anymore; the fight is now only about getting the last word.

record.grounding: Shows two children in a school corridor each blaming the other with 'always' and 'never', too busy preparing defences to listen.

row_description: Many read the chat and feel uneasy, but do not reply for fear of becoming the next target. Staying silent feels safe though it lets the rumour look like something everyone believes.
recipe_text: A diary or journal entry by the protagonist, written the same day, informal.

record.passage:
Saturday night
The class chat has been going crazy about Aadhya since afternoon. The screenshot, the laughing faces, the comments. I read every message. I didn't laugh. I felt sick, actually.
I typed "guys this is not okay" three times and deleted it three times. Because I know how it works. The second you defend someone, you're the next joke. Last year it was Pratik, just for one comment.
So I just watched. Forty-two people in the group and only eight are posting. The rest of us are like me, I bet. Quiet.
But when nobody says anything, it looks like everybody agrees. And Aadhya is seeing all of it.
Yash

qa.q: How many people are in the class chat?
qa.a: There are forty-two people in the group, and only eight are posting.

qa.q: What was Yash afraid of when deleting that message?
qa.a: Yash was afraid of becoming the next joke, like Pratik last year, if Yash defended Aadhya.

qa.q: What small step could Yash take at this stage?
qa.a: Yash could message Aadhya privately to show support, or quietly tell a trusted teacher, which does not make Yash a public target.

qa.q: What might Aadhya think on seeing the silence?
qa.a: Aadhya may feel the whole class believes the story, not knowing many readers feel uneasy too.

record.grounding: It shows a silent reader of a group chat who feels uneasy but stays quiet for fear of being targeted, while silence makes the rumour seem believed.

row_description: Mocking a sibling's failure, or running to tell on him, becomes a way to gain adult favour. Both lose, since the parent is tired and the sibling now has a real grievance.
recipe_text: Third-person narrative in a rural or small-town Indian setting (village, farm, kasba, local bus, temple fair, small shop).

record.passage: Evening in the village, and Sharmila had just come back from the fields, her feet dusty and her back aching. Before she could sit, Minakshi ran up. "Amma! Madhu broke the pot at the well and he fell in the mud, he looked so silly!" She laughed and flapped her arms like him falling. "And he didn't do his homework!" Madhu stood behind the door, his face red. Sharmila closed her eyes. "Minakshi, enough." Minakshi's smile faded. She had expected Amma to say, good girl for telling. Madhu glared at her and went to the back of the house. He didn't call her for their usual game of stones that night.

qa.q: What did Minakshi say Madhu broke?
qa.a: She said he broke the pot at the well.

qa.q: What did Minakshi expect when she told Amma?
qa.a: She expected Amma to praise her as a good girl for telling, wanting her mother's favour.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it?
qa.a: Mocking and reporting Madhu only tired Amma and hurt Madhu; Minakshi could say sorry to Madhu, and Amma could later talk to each child calmly and separately.

qa.q: How does Madhu feel after being mocked in front of Amma?
qa.a: He feels humiliated and angry, so he glares at his sister and skips their usual game of stones.

record.grounding: It illustrates a child mocking her brother and telling on him to gain adult favour, which only wearies the parent and gives the brother a real grievance.

row_description: The student turns up at the teacher's desk after school with doubts about becoming a doctor. She tests whether the teacher will take her seriously or laugh, and each respectful reply lowers her guard.
recipe_text: Third-person narrative set outside India (any country), ordinary everyday detail.

record.passage: Rain streaked the windows of the biology lab in Toronto. Rania lingered after the others left, pretending to wipe a bench that was already clean. Ms Jin looked up from her laptop. "Something on your mind?" "Kind of." Rania laughed, too quickly. "My parents think I'm going to med school. I'm not sure I even want to. Probably sounds dumb." "It doesn't." Ms Jin closed the laptop. "Tell me what you're not sure about." Rania talked for a minute, then stopped, checking her face. Ms Jin only nodded and waited. So Rania kept going, and this time she sat down.

qa.q: What was Rania pretending to do after class?
qa.a: She was pretending to wipe a bench that was already clean.

qa.q: What does Rania's quick laugh and "Probably sounds dumb" suggest?
qa.a: She is nervous about being judged and protects herself by mocking her own doubt before anyone else can.

qa.q: Which small move by Ms Jin lowered Rania's guard?
qa.a: Closing the laptop and asking what she wasn't sure about showed full attention and respect, so Rania felt safe to keep talking and sit down.

qa.q: If Ms Jin had joked about it, what would change for Rania?
qa.a: She would probably have left quickly and kept her doubts private, missing the chance to think them through with an adult she trusts.

record.grounding: A teenage girl tests whether her teacher will take her doubts about medicine seriously, and each respectful reply lowers her guard.
